For \(f(x)=\frac12\|x\|^2\), we have \(\nabla f(x)=x\), so each step is multiplication by
\[
A_k=I-\alpha_k P_k.
\]
The eigenvalues of \(A_k\) are
\[
1-\alpha_k,\qquad 1-4\alpha_k.
\]
Since \(0<\alpha_k\le \frac12\), the first eigenvalue is always positive. Thus \(A_k\) is singular exactly when
\[
\alpha_k=\frac14.
\]

The product is
\[
x_3=A_2A_1A_0x_0,
\]
so
\[
R(\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=\|A_2A_1A_0\|_2.
\]
Since a norm is nonnegative, the best possible value is at least \(0\). It remains to see whether the product can be made exactly zero.

Let \(u_k\) be the unit vector at angle \(k\pi/3\). When \(\alpha_k=\frac14\),
\[
A_k=\frac34\,u_ku_k^T,
\]
the rank-one projection onto the line spanned by \(u_k\), scaled by \(3/4\).

Take
\[
\alpha_0=\alpha_2=\frac14.
\]
Then
\[
A_2A_1A_0=0
\]
is equivalent to
\[
u_2^T A_1 u_0=0.
\]
Now \(A_1\) has eigenvalue \(1-\alpha_1\) along \(u_1\) and eigenvalue \(1-4\alpha_1\) along the perpendicular direction \(v_1\). Since
\[
u_0=\frac12u_1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}v_1,
\qquad
u_2=\frac12u_1+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}v_1,
\]
we get
\[
u_2^TA_1u_0
=
\frac14(1-\alpha_1)-\frac34(1-4\alpha_1)
=
\frac{-2+11\alpha_1}{4}.
\]
Thus \(u_2^TA_1u_0=0\) exactly when
\[
\alpha_1=\frac{2}{11}.
\]
This is admissible because \(0<2/11<1/2\). Therefore
\[
A_2A_1A_0=0,
\]
so \(R=0\).

Since \(R\ge0\) always, this is optimal. Hence
\[
\boxed{\left(R_*,(\alpha_0^*,\alpha_1^*,\alpha_2^*)\right)
=
\left(0,\left(\frac14,\frac{2}{11},\frac14\right)\right)}.
\]
